cover:
TIME: 2 min (0:00)
SAY: Welcome. This is an eight-week, hands-on Python series. No coding experience is needed, it is not for credit, and each week builds on the last. Today is about your project, not code.
DO: Introduce yourself and the other facilitators by name. Post the course site link in the chat. Ask people to turn cameras on if they are comfortable.
WATCH FOR: Late joiners. Do not restart for them; a facilitator catches them up in the chat.
arc:
TIME: 3 min
SAY: Here is the whole arc, one line per week. Today you finish a project card. Everything later builds on it. Topics may shift slightly after the planning survey.
DO: Read the table out in one pass. Point at row 1 (today). Do not explain later weeks in detail.
IF ASKED "Do I need to know Python?": No. Weeks 1 and 2 are written for absolute beginners.
ai:
TIME: 8 min (includes the live demo)
SAY: You will use AI every week. The skill is not typing code from memory. It is describing a task precisely, reading what the AI wrote, testing it on a small sample, and recording how you checked.
DO (live demo, 3 min): Open any AI chat. Paste a tiny made-up table (two or three rows with columns id, country, score). Then ask: "Using my table, show the average of the column called 'sentiment_score'." The column does not exist. The AI will usually invent code anyway. Read its answer aloud and ask: what would you not be able to tell from this answer?
SAY: A confident answer is not evidence. That is the whole course in one sentence.
WATCH FOR: If the AI says the column does not exist, that is fine: say "good, this time it caught it" and move on. Have a second prompt ready (ask for a column that is nearly right, like 'Score').
fails:
TIME: 4 min
SAY: Four ways AI code goes wrong. We practice catching each one. You do not need to memorize them.
DO: Read the four cards. For each, give one sentence of example: silent loss (rows quietly disappear), invented names (a column that does not exist), does something else (answers a different question), confident wrong explanations.
IF ASKED "Should I not use AI then?": Use it freely. The course is about checking it, not avoiding it.
week:
TIME: 3 min
SAY: Each week has a learning session, a coding session, and a little in between: required reading, a short practice page, and your verification log.
DO: Name the facilitators again and say what they do: they visit breakout rooms and watch the chat.
IF ASKED about the reading: The textbook sections are listed on the course site. Required, not graded.
WATCH FOR: Anxiety about workload. Say: the weekly work is designed to take a few hours, and you can always ask.
case:
TIME: 6 min (0:20)
SAY: Step 1: a case study. A specific topic in a specific context. Not "social media" but a named topic, place, and platform.
DO: Ask the room for one more example of a too-broad topic and help turn it into a case study live. Choose someone willing; do not cold-call.
WATCH FOR: People who say they have no topic yet. Say: pick something you care about for now. You can change it. There is a fallback dataset for anyone with no data.
question:
TIME: 7 min
SAY: Step 2: one main question and two or three sub-questions. The sub-questions break the big one into pieces you can answer.
DO: Read the mental-health example. For each sub-question, ask: what would you count or compute to answer this? Get one answer from the room.
IF ASKED "How many sub-questions?": Two or three. More than that and the project will be too big for eight weeks.
structures:
TIME: 6 min
SAY: Six structures to start from. These are starting points, not a checklist. Pick one that fits, mix, or use your own.
DO: Do not read the whole table. Name the six, then pick one row (comparative) and say when you would use it. Tell people the project guide has a worked example for each.
IF ASKED "Which is best?": None. Pick the one that fits your case study.
example:
TIME: 6 min (ends 0:45)
SAY: Here is one worked example with the Starbucks comments you will see in Week 2. Each sub-question maps to something we will teach: counting, sentiment, comparing groups.
DO: Read the main question and the three sub-questions. Point out the green label under each one: that is the skill. Ask: could you say what you would measure for each?
SAY: That is the test of a good sub-question.
doable:
TIME: 12 min (0:45 to 0:57)
SAY: Step 4: is it doable in eight weeks? Six quick checks. If you answer no or not sure to any, that tells you what to work on, it is not a failure.
DO: Go through the six cards. Spend longest on Data (what is one row?) and Measure (what would you count, label, or compute?). Read the too-big versus better example at the bottom. Pause for questions.
IF ASKED about ethics: Week 4 covers it properly. For now: is the data public, and could anyone be identified?
WATCH FOR: Ambitious projects. Say: it is fine to start big and narrow it. We will revise it together.
sharpen:
TIME: 5 min (0:57 to 1:02)
SAY: Step 5: use AI to sharpen your question, not to decide it. Paste in your question and ask it to critique, not to write.
DO: Show the prompt on screen and put it in the chat so people can copy it. Remind them: do not paste anything private. Then say: after it answers, write down what you accepted and what you rejected. That is your first verification log entry.
WATCH FOR: Students who let the AI rewrite their question completely. Say: it is your question. Keep your words.
task:
TIME: 3 min to introduce (1:02), then the activity (1:05 to 1:40), then 10 min to close (1:40 to 1:50)
SAY: Your task now: draft your project card. You finish when you have the four things on the right. 35 minutes, in pairs, in breakout rooms. Facilitators will visit.
DO: Put people in breakout rooms of two (or three). Share the card template link in the chat. Tell them the time and when you will call them back. Post a time check at 15 and 30 minutes.
SIGN-OFF (facilitators): Check each card for a case study, a main question with two or three sub-questions, what one row is plus a data source, and one thing to measure per sub-question. Anyone with no data picks the Starbucks or Lululemon file.
AT 1:40: Bring everyone back. Ask two or three volunteers to read their card. Thank them.
api:
TIME: 8 min (1:50 to 1:58)
SAY: One last thing before next time: what an API is. Think of ordering at a restaurant. You do not walk into the kitchen. You send an order in a fixed format and the dish comes back.
DO: Walk the three cards left to right: parameters are your order, the service is the kitchen, the response is the dish. No code today. Say: next session you will see this with real data.
IF ASKED "What is JSON?": Nested labeled data. You will practice reading it in the puzzle page.
next:
TIME: 2 min (1:58 to 2:00)
SAY: Next session is about how code thinks. Before then, read Chapter 3 sections 3.1 to 3.3 of the textbook, and finish your project card if you did not today. Creating a SerpAPI account is optional.
DO: Post the course site link again. Remind everyone to bring a laptop. Ask if anyone needs help with Google or Colab access, and invite them to message a facilitator privately.
CLOSE: Thank everyone. Facilitators stay for five minutes in case anyone has a question.
